title: On Spin Locks in AUTOSAR: Blocking Analysis of FIFO, Unordered, and Priority-Ordered Spin Locks

extraction.paper_name: On Spin Locks in AUTOSAR: Blocking Analysis of FIFO, Unordered, and Priority-Ordered Spin Locks
extraction.paper_description: This paper presents a comprehensive framework for worst-case blocking analysis of eight spin lock types (FIFO, unordered, priority-ordered with unordered/FIFO tie-breaking, each with preemptable/non-preemptable spinning) under partitioned fixed-priority (P-FP) scheduling. It introduces a novel mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) based approach to bound blocking, which is asymptotically less pessimistic than prior methods relying on execution cost inflation, by explicitly accounting for transitive delays and ensuring critical sections are not overcounted. The analysis is motivated by AUTOSAR spin lock requirements.

formal_description.statement:
A real-time workload consists of n sporadic tasks tau = {T_1, ..., T_n} scheduled on m identical processors P_1, ..., P_m. 
- e_i: Worst-Case Execution Time (WCET) of task T_i.
- p_i: Period of task T_i.
- J_i: A job of T_i.
- u_i = e_i / p_i: Utilization of task T_i.
- r_i: Worst-case response time of T_i.
- phi = max_i {p_i} / min_i {p_i}: Ratio of maximum and minimum period.
- P(T_i): Processor to which T_i is assigned.
- pi_i: Scheduling priority of T_i (lower value implies higher priority).
- Q = {q_1, ..., q_nr}: Set of n_r serially-reusable resources.
- N_i_q: Maximum number of times any job J_i accesses resource q.
- L_i_q: Maximum critical section length for T_i accessing q (L_i_q = 0 if N_i_q = 0).

variables.r_i: Worst-case response time of task T_i
variables.phi: Ratio of max to min task period
variables.N_i_q: Max accesses by T_i to resource q
variables.L_i_q: Max critical section length for T_i accessing q

assumptions: Implicit deadlines (D_i = p_i)
Tasks do not self-suspend
P-FP (Partitioned Fixed-Priority) scheduling
Jobs request and hold at most one resource at a time (no nested critical sections)
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the fundamental parameters and assumptions of the real-time system model.

informal_sketch.intuition: This defines the basic building blocks of our real-time system: tasks, their properties (execution time, period, priority), the processors they run on, and the shared resources they use. It also sets up key metrics like utilization and response time.
steps: Identify each task T_i with its WCET (e_i) and period (p_i).
Calculate task utilization u_i = e_i / p_i.
Assign each task T_i to a specific processor P(T_i) and a priority pi_i.
Define shared resources Q, and for each task T_i and resource q, specify the maximum number of accesses N_i_q and the maximum critical section length L_i_q.
The goal is to find r_i, the worst-case time from release to completion for any job of T_i.
key_insights: A clear system model is essential for any schedulability analysis.
Partitioned scheduling means tasks are statically assigned to processors.
Fixed-priority scheduling means tasks on a processor are ordered by priority.

formal_description.statement:
For local resources:
- Pi(q): Resource ceiling of a local resource q, defined as the highest priority among all tasks accessing q. Formally, Pi(q) = min_{T_i} {pi_i | N_i_q > 0}.
- Pi(t): Dynamic system ceiling at time t, defined as the highest resource ceiling of any resource in use at time t. Formally, Pi(t) = min_q {Pi(q) | q is locked at time t} U {n + 1} (where n + 1 indicates no resource is locked).

variables.Pi_q: Resource ceiling of local resource q
variables.N_i_q: Max accesses by T_i to resource q
variables.Pi_t: Dynamic system ceiling at time t

assumptions: Resources are local (shared only on a single processor)
Used in the context of the Multiprocessor Stack Resource Policy (MSRP)
formal_description.conclusion: Defines priority-based ceilings for local resources to manage access and prevent priority inversions.

informal_sketch.intuition: Resource ceilings are a mechanism to prevent deadlocks and bound blocking for local resources. Pi(q) is the 'danger level' of a resource, indicating the highest priority task that might use it. Pi(t) is the current 'danger level' of the system, reflecting resources currently held.
steps: For each local resource q, find all tasks T_i that access it (N_i_q > 0).
The resource ceiling Pi(q) is the highest priority (lowest pi_i value) among these tasks.
At any time t, the dynamic system ceiling Pi(t) is the highest Pi(q) of any resource q currently locked. If no resources are locked, it's a 'safe' value (n+1).
key_insights: Higher priority tasks have lower numerical priority values.
The SRP scheduling rule: a job J_i can only start if pi_i < Pi(t), ensuring resources it might need are available or can be acquired without blocking higher priority tasks.

formal_description.statement:
Under MSRP, jobs are subject to three types of blocking:
1.  beta_loc_i: Maximum local blocking incurred by job J_i. beta_loc_i = max_{T_l,q} {L_l_q | N_l_q > 0 AND Pi(q) <= pi_i < pi_l AND q is local}.
2.  S_i_q: Maximum spin time per request for global resource q by job J_i (for F|N locks). S_i_q = sum_{P_k != P(T_i)} max_{T_x} {L_x_q | P(T_x) = P_k} if N_i_q > 0, else 0.
3.  beta_rem_i: Maximum total remote blocking incurred by job J_i. beta_rem_i = sum_q N_i_q * S_i_q.
4.  e_h_inflated: Inflated execution cost of task T_h. e_h_inflated = e_h + beta_rem_h.
5.  beta_NP_i: Maximum non-preemptive blocking incurred by job J_i. beta_NP_i = max_{T_l,q} {S_l_q + L_l_q | P(T_i) = P(T_l) AND pi_i < pi_l AND q is global}.

variables.L_l_q: Max critical section length for T_l accessing q
variables.N_l_q: Max accesses by T_l to resource q
variables.Pi_q: Resource ceiling of local resource q
variables.S_i_q: Max spin time for T_i accessing q
variables.L_x_q: Max critical section length for T_x accessing q
variables.beta_rem_i: Max total remote blocking for T_i
variables.beta_rem_h: Max total remote blocking for T_h
variables.S_l_q: Max spin time for T_l accessing q

assumptions: MSRP (Multiprocessor Stack Resource Policy) is used
Non-preemptable FIFO-ordered spin locks (F|N locks) are used for global resources
formal_description.conclusion: Defines the specific blocking components and inflated execution costs used in the MSRP schedulability analysis.

informal_sketch.intuition: These definitions quantify different types of delays a task can experience due to resource contention under MSRP. Local blocking is from lower-priority tasks on the same processor holding local resources. Remote blocking is from tasks on *other* processors holding global resources, causing spinning. Non-preemptive blocking is from lower-priority tasks on the *same* processor holding global resources non-preemptably. Inflated execution costs are a way to account for remote blocking in the response time equation.
steps: To find beta_loc_i: Identify all local lower-priority tasks T_l on the same processor as T_i that access a local resource q whose ceiling Pi(q) is at least T_i's priority. The maximum L_l_q among these is beta_loc_i.
To find S_i_q (for F|N): For each processor P_k *other* than T_i's, find the maximum L_x_q of any task T_x on P_k that accesses q. Sum these maximums across all other processors.
To find beta_rem_i: Sum S_i_q for all requests T_i makes for global resources q (N_i_q * S_i_q).
To find e_h_inflated: Add T_h's WCET (e_h) and its total remote blocking (beta_rem_h).
To find beta_NP_i: Identify all local lower-priority tasks T_l on the same processor as T_i that access a global resource q. The maximum (S_l_q + L_l_q) among these is beta_NP_i.
key_insights: Blocking is categorized by resource type (local/global) and location (same/other processor).
FIFO spin locks provide strong progress guarantees, simplifying S_i_q calculation.
Inflating execution costs is a common, but potentially pessimistic, technique in prior work.

formal_description.statement:
Auxiliary sets and functions for the ILP-based analysis:
- tau_lh = {T_h | P(T_h) = P(T_i) AND pi_h < pi_i}: Set of local higher-priority tasks relative to T_i.
- tau_ll = {T_l | P(T_l) = P(T_i) AND pi_l > pi_i}: Set of local lower-priority tasks relative to T_i.
- Q_l: Set of local resources on processor P(T_i).
- Q_g: Set of global resources.
- pc(T_i) = {q | q in Q_l AND Pi(q) <= pi_i}: Conflict set of T_i, containing local resources with a priority ceiling at least T_i's priority.
- njobs(T_x, t) = ceil((t + r_x) / p_x): Upper bound on the number of jobs of T_x pending in any interval of length t.
- N_i_x_q = njobs(T_x, r_i) * N_x_q: Upper bound on the number of requests for q issued by jobs of T_x while a job of T_i is pending.
- tau_i = tau \ {T_i}: Set of all tasks except T_i.
- R_x_q_v: The v-th request of task T_x for resource q while J_i is pending.
- X_S_x_q_v: Blocking variable representing R_x_q_v's contribution to T_i's spin delay (X_S_x_q_v in [0, 1]).
- X_A_x_q_v: Blocking variable representing R_x_q_v's contribution to T_i's arrival blocking (X_A_x_q_v in [0, 1]).
- A_q: Binary indicator variable (0 or 1) for whether J_i incurred arrival blocking due to a critical section accessing q.
- ncs(T_i, q) = N_i_q + sum_{T_h in tau_lh} N_i_x_q: Upper bound on the number of requests for q issued by J_i itself or by preempting higher-priority jobs while J_i is pending (for F|N locks).
- tau_P_k = {T_x | P(T_x) = P_k}: Set of tasks assigned to processor P_k.

variables.tau_lh: Set of local higher-priority tasks for T_i
variables.tau_ll: Set of local lower-priority tasks for T_i
variables.Q_l: Set of local resources on P_T_i
variables.Pi_q: Resource ceiling of local resource q
variables.njobs_T_x_t: Max jobs of T_x pending in interval t
variables.N_i_x_q: Max requests by T_x for q while J_i pending
variables.N_x_q: Max accesses by T_x to resource q
variables.tau_i: Set of all tasks except T_i
variables.R_x_q_v: v-th request of T_x for q while J_i pending
variables.A_q: Binary indicator for arrival blocking by q
variables.ncs_T_i_q: Number of critical sections for T_i and higher-priority tasks for q
variables.N_i_q: Max accesses by T_i to resource q
variables.tau_P_k: Set of tasks on processor P_k

assumptions: Used in the context of the Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) for blocking analysis
njobs(T_x, t) assumes sporadic task model
formal_description.conclusion: Defines auxiliary sets, functions, and blocking variables crucial for formulating the MILP to compute blocking bounds.

informal_sketch.intuition: These definitions provide the vocabulary and tools for the new, more precise blocking analysis. We need to categorize tasks by priority and location, define how many jobs can be active, and introduce variables to track how much each critical section contributes to different types of blocking. The indicator variable A_q helps track if arrival blocking occurs for a specific resource.
steps: Group tasks into local higher-priority (tau_lh) and local lower-priority (tau_ll) sets relative to the task T_i being analyzed.
Define resource sets Q_l (local to T_i's processor) and Q_g (global).
Identify T_i's conflict set pc(T_i) for local resources.
Define njobs(T_x, t) to estimate the number of jobs of T_x that can be active over an interval t, which is used to calculate N_i_x_q, the total requests by T_x that could interfere with T_i.

Introduce continuous blocking variables X_S_x_q_v and X_A_x_q_v (between 0 and 1) to represent the fraction of a critical section's length that contributes to spin delay or arrival blocking, respectively.
Introduce a binary indicator A_q to mark if arrival blocking occurs due to resource q.
For F|N locks, define ncs(T_i, q) to count relevant critical sections for spin delay.
key_insights: The MILP approach uses continuous variables (X_S, X_A) to represent fractional blocking contributions, allowing for more fine-grained analysis.
The iterative nature of response time analysis means r_x values are estimates that converge to a fixed point.
The njobs function is critical for bounding the number of interfering requests over an interval.

formal_description.statement: Any blocking analysis relying on the inflation of job execution costs can be pessimistic by a factor of Omega(phi * n).

variables.phi: Ratio of maximum to minimum task period

assumptions: Analysis relies on inflating job execution costs (e.g., MSRP approach)
formal_description.conclusion: Such analyses can significantly overestimate blocking, leading to pessimistic schedulability results.

informal_sketch.intuition: Inflating a task's execution time to account for blocking means that if that task frequently preempts another, its 'inflated' blocking cost is counted repeatedly. This overcounts the actual blocking from individual critical sections, especially in systems with many tasks and wide period ranges.
steps: Consider a high-priority task T_h whose execution cost e_h is inflated by its remote blocking beta_rem_h.
When a lower-priority task T_i is analyzed, T_h's interference is calculated as (r_i / p_h) * e_h_inflated.
If T_h preempts T_i many times (r_i / p_h can be large, related to phi), the beta_rem_h component is added multiple times.
This leads to an overestimation of the total blocking, as a single critical section causing beta_rem_h is counted once per preemption, not just once for its actual duration.
key_insights: The core issue is that transitive blocking (a high-priority task spinning, thus delaying a lower-priority task) is accounted for by inflating WCETs.
Response-time analysis sums interference over multiple job releases, causing the inflated part to be summed multiple times.
This pessimism grows with the number of tasks (n) and the ratio of periods (phi).

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau: For all T_x in tau_i, for all q in Q, for all v: X_A_x_q_v + X_S_x_q_v <= 1.

variables.tau_i: Set of all tasks except T_i

assumptions: A single request R_x_q_v cannot simultaneously cause both spin delay and arrival blocking for J_i.
formal_description.conclusion: Each request R_x_q_v contributes at most its full critical section length (L_x_q) to either spin delay or arrival blocking, but not both simultaneously, for the task T_i being analyzed.

informal_sketch.intuition: A critical section can either cause a task to spin (spin delay) or block it upon release (arrival blocking), but not both at the exact same moment. If a job is spinning, it's already running. If it's arrival-blocked, it hasn't started yet. These are mutually exclusive states for the *same* critical section's impact on the *same* job at the *same* time.
steps: Identify a specific request R_x_q_v by task T_x for resource q.
Consider its impact on the analyzed task T_i.
If R_x_q_v causes T_i to spin (S1 or S2), T_i (or a higher-priority job) is active on its processor.
If R_x_q_v causes T_i to be arrival-blocked (A1 or A2), a lower-priority job is active on T_i's processor, and T_i is pending but not running.
These two scenarios cannot happen simultaneously for the same critical section's contribution to T_i's blocking.
key_insights: This constraint prevents double-counting the impact of a single critical section.
It reflects the fundamental mutual exclusivity of a job being 'active and spinning' versus 'pending and arrival-blocked'.

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau: sum_{q in Q} A_q <= 1.

variables.A_q: Binary indicator for arrival blocking by q

assumptions: A job J_i can incur arrival blocking at most once (upon release).
Jobs hold at most one resource at a time.
formal_description.conclusion: At most one resource can cause arrival blocking for a job J_i.

informal_sketch.intuition: Arrival blocking happens when a job is released and finds its processor occupied by a lower-priority task holding a resource. Since a job is released only once, and it can only be blocked by one lower-priority job holding one resource at that exact moment, only one resource can be the 'cause' of arrival blocking.
steps: A job J_i is released.
If it's arrival-blocked, it means a single lower-priority job J_l is executing on P(T_i) at that moment.
Since J_l holds at most one resource at a time, it can only be holding one resource q.
Therefore, only this single resource q can be responsible for J_i's arrival blocking.
key_insights: Arrival blocking is a 'one-time' event per job release.
The single-resource-holding assumption is key here.

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau: For all q in Q: A_q <= sum_{T_x in tau_ll} N_x_q.

variables.A_q: Binary indicator for arrival blocking by q
variables.tau_ll: Set of local lower-priority tasks for T_i
variables.N_x_q: Max accesses by T_x to resource q

assumptions: Arrival blocking for T_i due to resource q can only occur if q is accessed by at least one local lower-priority task.
formal_description.conclusion: If resource q causes arrival blocking (A_q = 1), then at least one local lower-priority task must access q.

informal_sketch.intuition: You can't be blocked by a resource that no one is using, or by a resource that only higher-priority tasks use (because they wouldn't block you upon release). Specifically, arrival blocking for T_i is caused by a *lower-priority* task on the *same processor* holding a resource. So, if A_q is 1, some T_x in tau_ll must access q.
steps: Assume A_q = 1, meaning T_i is arrival-blocked by resource q.
By definition of arrival blocking, this must be caused by a local lower-priority job J_l holding q.
This implies that T_l (the task of J_l) must be in tau_ll and must access q (N_l_q > 0).
Therefore, the sum of N_x_q for T_x in tau_ll must be greater than 0.
key_insights: This constraint ensures that arrival blocking is only attributed to resources that can actually cause it.
It filters out impossible blocking scenarios based on task access patterns and priorities.

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau: For all q in Q_l \ pc(T_i): A_q <= 0.

variables.Q_l: Set of local resources on P(T_i)
variables.A_q: Binary indicator for arrival blocking by q

assumptions: Arrival blocking for T_i due to a local resource q (condition A2) is only possible if q is in T_i's conflict set pc(T_i).
formal_description.conclusion: Local resources not in T_i's conflict set cannot cause arrival blocking for T_i.

informal_sketch.intuition: The conflict set pc(T_i) contains local resources whose ceiling is high enough to block T_i. If a local resource q is *not* in pc(T_i), it means its ceiling is lower than T_i's priority. According to SRP rules, T_i would not be blocked by such a resource upon release, even if a lower-priority task holds it.
steps: Identify local resources q on P(T_i) that are *not* in pc(T_i).
For such a resource q, its resource ceiling Pi(q) must be strictly greater than pi_i (meaning T_i has higher priority than Pi(q)).
The SRP rule states J_i can start if pi_i < Pi(t). If Pi(q) > pi_i, then J_i would not be blocked by q.
Therefore, A_q must be 0 for such resources.
key_insights: This constraint leverages the properties of the SRP to refine arrival blocking possibilities.
It eliminates scenarios where T_i would not be blocked by local resources due to priority ceiling rules.

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau: sum_{T_x in tau_lh} sum_q sum_{v=1 to N_i_x_q} X_A_x_q_v <= 0.

variables.tau_lh: Set of local higher-priority tasks for T_i
variables.N_i_x_q: Max requests by T_x for q while J_i pending

assumptions: Arrival blocking (conditions A1 and A2) requires a lower-priority job to be scheduled on P(T_i) at the time of J_i's release.
formal_description.conclusion: Requests from local higher-priority tasks cannot cause arrival blocking for T_i.

informal_sketch.intuition: Arrival blocking means T_i is ready but can't run because a *lower-priority* task is holding the processor. Higher-priority tasks, by definition, would preempt T_i if T_i were running, or would not be running if T_i were ready and they were not. They cannot be the cause of T_i being blocked *upon release*.
steps: Arrival blocking conditions A1 and A2 explicitly state that a *lower-priority* job must be scheduled on P(T_i) at the time of J_i's release.
Tasks in tau_lh have *higher* priority than T_i.
Therefore, a job of T_x in tau_lh cannot be the cause of J_i's arrival blocking.
key_insights: This constraint directly enforces the priority-based nature of arrival blocking.
It simplifies the ILP by eliminating a class of impossible blocking scenarios.

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau: For all q in Q: sum_{T_x in tau_ll} sum_{v=1 to N_i_x_q} X_A_x_q_v <= A_q.

variables.tau_ll: Set of local lower-priority tasks for T_i
variables.N_i_x_q: Max requests by T_x for q while J_i pending
variables.A_q: Binary indicator for arrival blocking by q

assumptions: If A_q = 0, no request for q causes arrival blocking for J_i.
If A_q = 1, at most one request for q can cause arrival blocking for J_i (due to Constraint 2 and single resource holding).
formal_description.conclusion: The total arrival blocking contribution from requests for resource q by local lower-priority tasks cannot exceed the indicator A_q (which is 0 or 1).

informal_sketch.intuition: This constraint links the individual blocking variables (X_A) to the overall indicator (A_q). If A_q is 0, no X_A for that resource can be positive. If A_q is 1, it means *some* request for q caused arrival blocking, but due to Constraint 2 and the single-resource holding assumption, only one such request can be active at the moment of blocking. So, the sum of X_A for q should be at most 1 (representing one critical section's length).
steps: Case 1: A_q = 0. By definition, no request for q causes arrival blocking. Thus, all X_A_x_q_v for this q must be 0, making their sum 0. The constraint 0 <= 0 holds.

Case 2: A_q = 1. By definition, J_i incurred arrival blocking due to q. This means one specific request R_l_q_v from a local lower-priority task T_l was active. This R_l_q_v would contribute 1 to X_A_l_q_v. All other X_A for q would be 0. The sum would be 1. The constraint 1 <= 1 holds.
It's impossible for the sum of X_A_x_q_v to be > 1 because only one critical section can be in progress on P(T_i) at J_i's release (Constraint 2).
key_insights: This constraint ensures consistency between the detailed blocking variables and the high-level indicator.
It implicitly uses the single-resource-holding and single-arrival-blocking event properties.

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau: sum_{T_x in tau_ll U tau_lh} sum_q sum_{v=1 to N_i_x_q} X_S_x_q_v <= 0.

variables.tau_ll: Set of local lower-priority tasks for T_i
variables.tau_lh: Set of local higher-priority tasks for T_i
variables.N_i_x_q: Max requests by T_x for q while J_i pending

assumptions: Spin delay (conditions S1 and S2) occurs when a job on P(T_i) is busy-waiting for a resource held by a *remote* task.
A job cannot be simultaneously spinning and executing a critical section on the same processor.
formal_description.conclusion: Requests from local tasks (on the same processor as T_i) cannot cause spin delay for T_i.

informal_sketch.intuition: Spin delay happens when a task on P(T_i) (either T_i itself or a higher-priority task preempting T_i) tries to acquire a global resource that is held by a task on *another* processor. It's impossible to spin waiting for a resource held by a task on your *own* processor, because that would imply two tasks are running simultaneously on one processor, or a task is spinning for itself, which is nonsensical.
steps: Spin delay conditions S1 and S2 imply that the job on P(T_i) is busy-waiting.

If a local task T_x (from tau_ll or tau_lh) were holding the resource q, then the job on P(T_i) would either be T_x (executing q) or T_i (or T_h) would be blocked by T_x (arrival blocking or preemption, not spinning).
It's impossible for a job on P(T_i) to be spinning for a resource held by another job on P(T_i).
Therefore, all X_S_x_q_v for local tasks T_x must be 0.
key_insights: Spinning is inherently an inter-processor synchronization mechanism.
This constraint formalizes the distinction between local and remote blocking mechanisms.

formal_description.statement: In any schedule of tau with F|N locks: For all P_k, for all q: sum_{T_x in tau_P_k} sum_{v=1 to N_i_x_q} X_S_x_q_v <= ncs(T_i, q).

variables.tau_P_k: Set of tasks on processor P_k
variables.N_i_x_q: Max requests by T_x for q while J_i pending
variables.ncs_T_i_q: Number of critical sections for T_i and higher-priority tasks for q

assumptions: FIFO-ordered Non-Preemptable (F|N) spin locks are used.
Strong progress guarantee of FIFO spin locks.
formal_description.conclusion: The total spin delay contribution for resource q from all tasks on any processor P_k (including T_i's processor) is bounded by the total number of critical sections for q issued by T_i itself or by preempting higher-priority jobs.

informal_sketch.intuition: For FIFO spin locks, requests are served in the order they arrive. If T_i (or a higher-priority task preempting T_i) makes a request for q, it will eventually get the lock. The number of times it can be delayed by *other* tasks' requests for q is limited. This constraint says that the total 'spin delay' for a resource q, across all tasks on any given processor, cannot exceed the total number of times T_i (or its local higher-priority tasks) *could* request that resource while T_i is active.
steps: Consider a specific resource q.
ncs(T_i, q) represents the maximum number of times T_i or its local higher-priority tasks will request q while T_i is pending.
Due to FIFO ordering, each of these ncs(T_i, q) requests will eventually be served.
Any spin delay for q must be caused by one of these ncs(T_i, q) requests waiting for a lock.
Therefore, the sum of spin delay contributions (X_S) for resource q from all tasks on any processor P_k cannot exceed ncs(T_i, q).
key_insights: This constraint is specific to FIFO spin locks, leveraging their strong ordering guarantee.
It bounds the total 'work' of spinning for a resource based on the number of relevant requests.
The proof relies on the pigeon-hole principle, ensuring that if more than ncs(T_i, q) requests caused spin delay, at least one request would have been served out of FIFO order, which is impossible.

formal_description.statement: The optimization objective is to maximize b_i, where b_i = sum_{T_x in tau_i} sum_{q in Q} sum_{v=1 to N_i_x_q} (X_S_x_q_v + X_A_x_q_v) * L_x_q.

variables.tau_i: Set of all tasks except T_i
variables.N_i_x_q: Max requests by T_x for q while J_i pending
variables.L_x_q: Max critical section length for T_x accessing q

assumptions: X_A_x_q_v in [0, 1] and X_S_x_q_v in [0, 1] for each R_x_q_v.
Constraints 1-8 (and others for specific lock types) define the feasible region for the blocking variables.
formal_description.conclusion: This objective function, when maximized subject to the constraints, yields a safe upper bound on the worst-case cumulative blocking incurred by any job of task T_i.

informal_sketch.intuition: The goal of the blocking analysis is to find the absolute worst-case total blocking (b_i) that task T_i can experience. This is achieved by summing up the contributions of all possible critical sections from other tasks (T_x) that could block T_i, weighted by their lengths (L_x_q) and their blocking variables (X_S, X_A). The MILP finds the combination of blocking variable values that maximizes this sum while respecting all the rules (constraints) of the system.

The total blocking b_i is the sum of (X_S_x_q_v + X_A_x_q_v) * L_x_q for all relevant requests.

An MILP solver is used to find the maximum possible value of b_i, subject to all defined constraints (e.g., Constraint 1 ensures X_S + X_A <= 1, so a critical section's length is not counted more than once).

formal_description.statement:
Under the MSRP, a safe bound on T_i's maximum response time r_i is given by a solution to the following recurrence:
r_i = e_i + beta_rem_i + max(beta_NP_i, beta_loc_i) + sum_{T_h in tau_lh} ceil(r_i / p_h) * e_h_inflated.

variables.beta_rem_i: Max total remote blocking for T_i
variables.tau_lh: Set of local higher-priority tasks for T_i

assumptions: MSRP scheduling protocol is used.
Non-preemptable FIFO-ordered spin locks are used for global resources.
Response time analysis is used to check schedulability.
formal_description.conclusion: This recurrence relation can be solved iteratively to find the worst-case response time r_i for task T_i under MSRP.

informal_sketch.intuition: A task's worst-case response time is its own execution time plus any blocking it experiences (local, remote, non-preemptive) and any interference from higher-priority tasks on the same processor. The MSRP analysis accounts for remote blocking by inflating the execution times of higher-priority tasks.
steps: Start with an initial estimate for r_i (e.g., r_i = e_i).
Calculate beta_rem_i, beta_NP_i, beta_loc_i, and e_h_inflated for all tasks.
Iteratively update r_i using the formula: new_r_i = e_i + beta_rem_i + max(beta_NP_i, beta_loc_i) + sum_{T_h in tau_lh} ceil(r_i / p_h) * e_h_inflated.
Repeat until r_i converges (new_r_i == r_i) or exceeds p_i.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_MSRP_response_time(task_i, tasks, resources, num_processors):
    r_i_current = task_i.e # Initial estimate
    r_i_next = 0
    
    # Pre-calculate blocking terms and inflated WCETs (these depend on other tasks' r_h, so might need outer iteration)
    beta_rem_i = calculate_beta_rem_i(task_i, resources, tasks, num_processors)
    beta_NP_i = calculate_beta_NP_i(task_i, tasks, resources, num_processors)
    beta_loc_i = calculate_beta_loc_i(task_i, tasks, resources)
    
    e_h_inflated_map = {t.id: calculate_e_h_inflated(t, resources, tasks, num_processors) for t in tasks}

    while True:
        interference = 0
        tau_lh = get_local_higher_priority_tasks(task_i, tasks)
        for task_h in tau_lh:
            interference += math.ceil(r_i_current / task_h.p) * e_h_inflated_map[task_h.id]
        
        r_i_next = task_i.e + beta_rem_i + max(beta_NP_i, beta_loc_i) + interference
        
        if r_i_next == r_i_current:
            break
        if r_i_next > task_i.p: # Deadline miss
            return r_i_next
        r_i_current = r_i_next
        
    return r_i_current
key_insights: This is a standard fixed-point iteration for response time analysis.
The blocking terms (beta_rem, beta_NP, beta_loc) are added directly.
Interference from higher-priority tasks is calculated based on their inflated execution costs.

formal_description.statement:
A safe upper bound on T_i's maximum response time r_i is given by a solution to the following recurrence:
r_i = e_i + b_i + I_i(r_i).
Where I_i(r_i) = sum_{T_h in tau_lh} ceil(r_i / p_h) * e_h.

variables.b_i: Total blocking for T_i (from ILP objective)
variables.I_i_r_i: Worst-case interference from local higher-priority jobs
variables.tau_lh: Set of local higher-priority tasks for T_i

assumptions: P-FP scheduling.
Blocking term b_i is computed using the MILP approach.
This recurrence does not rely on inflated execution costs.
formal_description.conclusion: This recurrence relation can be solved iteratively to find the worst-case response time r_i for task T_i using the MILP-derived blocking term.

informal_sketch.intuition: Similar to the MSRP recurrence, a task's response time is its own execution plus blocking and interference. However, this new approach separates the blocking (b_i) from the interference (I_i), and crucially, the interference term uses the *actual* WCET (e_h) of higher-priority tasks, not an inflated one. This avoids the pessimism identified in Theorem 1.
steps: Start with an initial estimate for r_i (e.g., r_i = e_i).
For the current r_i values of all tasks, compute b_i for T_i using the MILP (which depends on r_x for N_i_x_q and njobs).
Calculate I_i(r_i) using the current r_i and the actual WCETs of local higher-priority tasks.
Update r_i using the formula: new_r_i = e_i + b_i + I_i(r_i).
Repeat until r_i converges (new_r_i == r_i) or exceeds p_i. This is an iterative process where b_i and r_i are determined in alternating fashion until a fixpoint is reached.
informal_sketch.pseudocode:
def calculate_ILP_response_time(task_i, all_tasks, all_resources):
    r_i_current = task_i.e # Initial estimate
    r_i_next = 0
    
    # Outer loop for fixed-point iteration of all response times
    # In a full implementation, this would be part of a larger iterative solver
    # where all r_x are updated until convergence.
    
    while True: # Response time iteration for task_i
        # 1. Calculate b_i using MILP (conceptually, this depends on current r_x for all tasks)
        #    For this sketch, assume a function `solve_milp_for_b_i` exists.
        #    This function would take current r_values for all tasks to compute N_i_x_q.
        b_i_val = solve_milp_for_b_i(task_i, all_tasks, all_resources, current_r_values_map)

        # 2. Calculate interference I_i(r_i)
        interference = 0
        tau_lh = get_local_higher_priority_tasks(task_i, all_tasks)
        for task_h in tau_lh:
            interference += math.ceil(r_i_current / task_h.p) * task_h.e
        
        r_i_next = task_i.e + b_i_val + interference
        
        if r_i_next == r_i_current:
            break
        if r_i_next > task_i.p: # Deadline miss
            return r_i_next
        r_i_current = r_i_next
        
    return r_i_current
key_insights: This is the core response time equation for the improved analysis.
The separation of blocking (b_i) and interference (I_i) is key to reducing pessimism.
The interference term uses actual WCETs, avoiding the overcounting issue.

formal_description.statement: A task T_i is schedulable if its worst-case response time r_i is less than or equal to its period p_i (assuming implicit deadlines). Formally, T_i is schedulable if r_i <= p_i.
assumptions: Implicit deadlines (D_i = p_i).
r_i is a safe upper bound on the actual worst-case response time.
formal_description.conclusion: Task T_i meets its deadline and is thus schedulable.

informal_sketch.intuition: The fundamental goal of real-time scheduling is to ensure all tasks complete their work before their deadlines. For implicit-deadline tasks, the deadline is simply the period. So, if the worst-case time a task takes to finish (its response time) is less than or equal to its period, it's schedulable.
steps: Calculate the worst-case response time r_i for task T_i using either the MSRP or ILP recurrence.
Compare r_i with T_i's period p_i.
If r_i <= p_i, the task is schedulable.
If r_i > p_i, the task is not schedulable (it misses its deadline in the worst case).
key_insights: This is the ultimate test for real-time system predictability.
The accuracy of r_i directly impacts the confidence in schedulability.
